manuscript_title: Alternate RNA decoding results in stable and abundant proteins in mammals

required_revisions.text: Re-run all RAAS dotplot comparisons (Fig. 4b,c, Fig. 5c, Extended Data Fig. 5) with Benjamini-Hochberg correction applied within explicitly defined analysis families. Report the family size (number of tests) for each family in the Methods, update all significance cutoffs and figure legends to corrected q-values, and state in the Results which previously significant comparisons no longer survive correction.

Scale the tissue-type and cancer-specificity claims to whatever survives step 1. If a substantial fraction of comparisons lose significance, revise the Abstract wording ('strong tissue-type and cancer specificity') and the corresponding Results/Discussion statements to descriptive or exploratory framing, and say so explicitly rather than leaving the original phrasing intact.

Remove causal language about protein stability driving high RAAS from the Abstract, Results heading and Discussion, replacing it with association language, and add a Discussion paragraph enumerating the detection/selection-bias and reverse-causality alternatives. State explicitly that the shared-peptide analysis (Fig. 3e,f) is conditional on SAAP detection and does not escape upstream detectability filtering, and name the perturbation experiments (e.g. synonymous codon engineering, targeted mutagenesis) that would be needed to establish causation.

Disclose the family size for the tissue-enrichment FDR correction (Extended Data Fig. 5h,i) in Methods — the correction itself is documented in the manuscript and is not in question, only its reported scope.

Add a supplemental table documenting the LSCC genomic comparison: variant-calling pipeline, sample size, matching procedure and result, cited at the point in Results where the claim that patient mutations did not correspond to identified AAS is made.

Add the table (or figure panel) reporting the number of proteins with median RAAS>1, >0.5 and >0.1, computed separately for the full 8,801-site set and the 2,000 high-confidence subset, and clarify in the text how the 360-protein figure is derived and how sensitive it is to the confidence threshold.

Report effect sizes alongside p-values as proposed: eta-squared with 95% CI for each ANOVA factor (Fig. 4f, Fig. 5m), Spearman rho with 95% CI and codon counts per RAAS quartile (Fig. 5k), and n (SAAP/proteins) for each degradation-rate correlation (Fig. 3d, Extended Data Fig. 3m,n).

Report the full distribution (median, IQR, 95% CI) of test-set Pearson correlations across the 1000 XGBoost retrainings, state explicitly that hyperparameter tuning used training-fold cross-validation only, and add a null baseline (global median RAAS) for comparison with r=0.44.

Specify the XGBoost hyperparameters actually used (learning rate, max depth, n_estimators, subsampling, or an explicit statement that R defaults were used) and state whether random seeds were set for the 1000 retrainings and 100 leave-one-factor-out runs; deposit seeds or the seed-setting code in the GitHub repository.

Provide a resolvable public repository accession for the MS data used, or state clearly for each dataset which existing accession it corresponds to (PXD010154, PXD030983 are given; CPTAC PDC study identifiers should be listed individually rather than only as a portal URL). Do the same for the CPTAC RNA-seq data.

State the RNA-seq library-preparation kit (vendor and catalogue number) for data generated for this study, or state explicitly that all RNA-seq data are reanalysed public datasets and cite the source publication where the library prep is described.

Add the Discussion paragraph comparing the stability-based mechanism to the stress/starvation-induced substitution mechanism of Pataskar et al. (2022) and Yang et al., stating specifically which of the two the degradation-rate data can and cannot distinguish.

Add DOIs or PMIDs for References 1 (Cantwell-Dorris et al. 2011), 3 (Wright & Vissel 2012), 17 (Karijolich & Yu 2011) and 38 (McCormick et al. 2024 preprint). For Reference 17, clarify in the text whether the cited work addresses sense-codon recoding or only stop-codon readthrough, since the Discussion argument depends on which.

minor_suggestions: Add the Introduction paragraph stating the two central hypotheses, and the one-sentence formal definition of 'alternate translation', as proposed in the rebuttal.

Consider matching the Abstract's cross-species wording to the appropriately hedged Results text: the 55-site overlap is framed in Results as a detectability-limited lower bound, and the Abstract should not read more strongly than that.
Cite the Wisniewski et al. justification for the 30x10^6 histone copies/cell value and include the proposed +/-50% sensitivity analysis in Extended Data.

State the replication structure for both the CPTAC TMT and label-free datasets (technical/biological replicates per sample, whether replicates were averaged), even if this is inherited from the source studies.
Add an environment specification (renv.lock, requirements.txt, or Dockerfile) to the GitHub repository, and record library versions for the Python components where these are currently unstated.
Specify the exact gnomAD query/filtering criteria used, or deposit the queried variant subset, so the constraint analysis can be reproduced against a fixed snapshot.
Name the MS instrument models for the reanalysed datasets, or state that these vary by source study and point to the relevant table.

weaknesses.text: The central claim that alternatively translated proteoforms are 'the most abundant protein products for 360 proteins' (Abstract and Results) rests on the interpretation of RAAS > 1 as evidence that the substituted form dominates. However, the authors cannot fully exclude the possibility that some high-RAAS observations result from undetected genetic polymorphisms (despite filtering against gnomAD, they acknowledge 'polymorphisms cannot account for the substitutions'), combinatorial modifications on the same peptide adding up to the observed mass shift, or systematic biases in peptide ionization or detectability that differ between substituted and base peptides in ways not captured by their models. The authors address each concern individually (Extended Data Fig. 2d-i shows ionization and detectability are similar), but the cumulative case that high RAAS reflects true proteoform dominance rather than a measurement artifact or confound is circumstantial. What would definitively rule out the hypothesis that most high-RAAS observations reflect undetected genetic variants or combinatorial modifications rather than alternate translation?

The manuscript does not state its central contribution explicitly in the Introduction or early Results. The reader must infer from the Abstract and scattered statements that the paper's main claim is that (1) alternate translation produces thousands of abundant proteins, and (2) protein stability explains why some substitutions accumulate despite low synthesis rates. This should be stated as a clear hypothesis before the results section, not left implicit.

Figure 1 is dense and difficult to parse without extensive caption reading; the workflow diagram would benefit from clearer labeling of decision points (e.g., which filters remove which candidates) and the relationship between the dependent peptide search and validation search is not immediately clear from the figure alone.

The term 'alternate translation' is used throughout but is never formally defined in the main text; readers must infer from context that it means 'translation deviating from the genetic code' but the exact mechanisms (wobble pairing, tRNA mischarging, codon recoding via RNA modifications) are discussed only later and not unified under a single clear definition.

The claim that RAAS values are 'positively associated with intrinsically disordered regions' (Abstract) is supported by Fig. 5h but the effect size and statistical significance are not stated in the main text, only in the figure legend.

The paper identifies 60,803 spectra corresponding to 8,801 unique substitution sites but then focuses analysis on 2,000 high-confidence sites; the relationship between these numbers and how they relate to the 360 proteins with RAAS > 1 is not clearly explained in the Results section.

The conservation analysis (Fig. 5l-m) identifies only 55 identical SAAP sequences between human and mouse despite analyzing thousands of sites; the authors acknowledge this likely underestimates true conservation but do not quantify how much of the apparent lack of conservation is due to technical factors (peptide detectability, sequence homology) versus true biological divergence.

questions: Can the authors provide a quantitative estimate of how many of the high-RAAS substitutions would be expected if the observed mass shifts resulted from undetected genetic variants at frequencies below the gnomAD detection threshold, or from combinatorial modifications?

In Fig. 2e, the shared peptide abundance for RAAS > 1 is claimed to be 'closer to SAAP abundance than BP abundance,' but no quantitative measure of 'closeness' (e.g., fold-difference, correlation coefficient) is provided; what is the actual magnitude of this effect?

The authors state that 'for about half of all spectra matched to SAAP, the measured mass shift indicating a substitution is localized with high confidence to a single position' but do not specify whether the high-RAAS substitutions are enriched in this high-confidence subset or distributed across both high- and low-confidence groups.

weaknesses.text: **Multiple-comparison correction is applied inconsistently and incompletely.** The authors use Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction for GO enrichment (Methods, 'Protein set enrichment analysis') and Pfam domain analysis, but do not disclose whether they corrected for the many statistical tests across the main results. Figure 4b,c and Extended Data Fig. 5 show RAAS dotplots comparing distributions across hundreds of substitution types and amino acid properties using Student's t-tests; the Methods state 'two-sided Student's t-tests' but do not state how many tests were run, whether a family-wise correction was applied, or what the corrected threshold is. The paper reports p-values as 'p≤10^−10' and 'p<10^−15' throughout (e.g., Fig. 5b, Extended Data Fig. 5h,i) without disclosing the family size or correction method. This is a HARD issue: without knowing the number of tests and the correction applied, the reader cannot assess whether these p-values are credible. The authors should state the total number of substitution-type comparisons, the correction method, and the corrected significance threshold.

**The XGBoost RAAS prediction model (Fig. 5i) lacks proper validation reporting.** The Methods state 'The data was randomly split into a train fraction, 80%, and a test fraction, 20%' and 'The model was retrained 1000 times on random subsets of test and train data,' but do not disclose: (1) whether hyperparameters were tuned on the test set (leakage risk); (2) the distribution of performance across the 1000 retrainings (only a median is shown); (3) whether the reported Pearson correlation of 0.44 is the median, mean, or a single run; (4) the baseline model used for comparison. The caption states 'Each feature used increases the model's predictive power (bottom panel)' but does not define how feature importance was computed or whether it was derived from the same test set. A correlation of 0.44 on test data is modest; the paper should report 95% CIs on the correlation across folds and compare against a null model (e.g., predicting median RAAS for all proteins).

**The gnomAD constraint analysis (Fig. 5j,k) lacks a formal statistical test and effect-size reporting.** The text states 'Missense variants are less constrained with increasing RAAS (p<10^−4)' but does not name the test (Spearman? linear regression?), the sample size (number of codons?), or the effect size (slope, Spearman ρ?). The Methods describe computing observed/expected ratios and comparing control groups but do not state the test statistic or degrees of freedom. The p-value alone does not establish the magnitude of the association; a correlation of 0.1 and 0.8 can both be 'significant' in large samples. Report the effect size (ρ or β) with 95% CI.

**The degradation-rate analysis (Fig. 3c–f) does not disclose the sample size or statistical power.** The text states 'Many substituted peptides have lower degradation rates than their non-substituted counterparts' and 'strong inverse correlation (p<10^−10)' but does not report n (number of SAAP? number of proteins? number of cells?). The Methods state 'Degradation rates (α) were computed as the slope of ln(1+h/l)=αt' but do not specify how many time points were used per peptide, whether replicates were averaged before regression, or whether the regression was weighted. Figure 3d shows a scatter plot with apparent heteroscedasticity; were the data log-transformed? The correlation is reported for 'primary hepatocytes' and separately for 'B cells and natural killer cells' (Extended Data Fig. 3m,n) but the sample sizes and test statistics are not given. State n and the regression method for each cell type.

**The ANOVA model (Fig. 4f) does not report effect sizes or confidence intervals.** The figure shows F-values and p-values but not the proportion of variance explained (η² or ω²) or 95% CIs on the effect sizes. The text states 'substitution type explains the most variance' but does not quantify 'most'—is it 30% or 70%? Report η² with 95% CI for each factor.

**Tissue-type enrichment analysis (Extended Data Fig. 5h,i) applies FDR correction but does not disclose the family size or the corrected threshold.** The Methods state 'p-values were adjusted with a Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction to get q-values' and 'Substitution types were considered significantly enriched...if...q-value of ≤0.01' but do not state how many substitution-type × tissue comparisons were tested. If there are 255 unique substitutions (stated in Results) and 4 tissues, that is ~1000 tests; the corrected threshold should be much lower than 0.01 if Benjamini-Hochberg was applied at family-wise α=0.05. Clarify the family size and verify the corrected threshold.

**The tumor vs. normal tissue comparison (Fig. 5b) does not disclose the sample size or multiple-comparison correction.** The volcano plot shows substitution types with significantly different RAAS in tumor vs. matched normal tissue, but the Methods state 'p-values were FDR-adjusted into q-values using the Benjamini-Hochberg method' without naming the family size (number of substitution types tested?). The text does not report how many patient pairs were included or whether the paired t-test was the appropriate test (are the RAAS values normally distributed within each substitution type?). Report n (number of substitution types and patient pairs) and the corrected significance threshold.

**The RNA modification overlap test (Supplemental Fig. 8a) uses a hypergeometric test but does not disclose the multiple-comparison correction or the prior probability of overlap.** The Methods state 'we used a cumulative hypergeometric distribution test (p[X>179], in R: phyper...)' and report p<10^−10, but do not state whether this p-value was corrected for testing multiple RNA modifications or whether the test was one-sided or two-sided. The text states 'uracil modifications overlap significantly (p<10^−10) with substitution sites' but does not report the observed and expected counts or the odds ratio. Report the counts, the odds ratio with 95% CI, and whether a Bonferroni or other correction was applied if multiple modifications were tested.

questions: How many total statistical tests were run across Figures 4b,c and Extended Data Fig. 5, and what was the family-wise correction applied?
For the XGBoost model, were hyperparameters (tree depth, learning rate, etc.) tuned on the test set, and what is the 95% CI on the test-set correlation across the 1000 retrainings?
For the gnomAD constraint analysis, what is the Spearman ρ or regression slope with 95% CI, and how many codons were included in each RAAS quartile?
For the degradation-rate analysis, what is n (number of SAAP, proteins, or cell replicates) for each cell type, and were the data log-transformed before regression?

weaknesses.text: The authors do not adequately engage with Pataskar et al. (2022) on tryptophan-to-phenylalanine substitutions under amino acid starvation, which directly competes with the claim that high-abundance substitutions reflect protein stabilization rather than synthesis rates alone; the manuscript cites Pataskar et al. only in passing as evidence that substitutions occur under stress, not as a competing mechanistic explanation.

The statement 'Mutations in the genomes of LSCC patients did not correspond to any of the identified AAS' is asserted without showing data, supplemental tables, or methodological details (sample size, variant-calling pipeline, matching threshold), making the claim unverifiable from the text alone.

The claim that U modifications overlap significantly with substitution sites (p < 10^−10) lacks specification of which U modifications are involved and does not provide effect sizes; the authors acknowledge they 'cannot confidently rule out the possibility of multiple modifications or alternate events,' undercutting the mechanistic claim.

The claim that 'the prevalence and stability of alternatively translated proteins are presumed low' in microorganisms cites ref. 12 (Wright & Vissel on AMPA receptors), which does not address microorganisms—this appears to be a citation error.

The authors cite Netzer et al. (2009) for the claim that 'non-cognate amino acid acylation may confer beneficial functions,' but the abstract focuses on oxidative stress and translational fidelity, not functional benefits of mischarging—the citation support is unclear.

The claim that 'previous reports of substitutions did not test if they have genetic origin' is unsupported by specific references; Mordret et al. (2019) did address genetic origin in yeast, so this claim needs clarification.

The histone ruler method (Wiśniewski et al. 2014) is cited for copy-number estimation without discussing the assumption that histone abundance is constant across tissues and cell types, which may not hold in cancer.
The CPTAC datasets are cited without specifying version, release date, or dataset identifiers, making reproducibility harder.
The Oktoberfest rescoring pipeline is cited as validation but the authors do not report FDR or sensitivity on SAAP sequences specifically, leaving confidence in the re-scoring step unclear.

The claim that 'substitutions of polar amino acids have consistently higher RAAS than substitutions of other amino acid types' is supported by figures but the authors do not explain why polar amino acids would be preferentially misread or stabilized, leaving the mechanism unclear.

questions: Does the filtering of peptides that could be explained by both an AAS and a PTM (e.g., Q→E, N→D as deamidation) remove true substitutions that happen to overlap with known PTMs, and how many SAAP were discarded on this basis?

For the claim that 'mutations in the genomes of LSCC patients did not correspond to any of the identified AAS,' please provide the supplemental table or figure showing the variant-calling results and the matching procedure used to exclude genetic origin.

The degradation-rate analysis is restricted to three cell types (hepatocytes, B cells, NK cells); do the authors have SILAC data from other tissues (e.g., cancer cell lines) that would allow testing whether the stabilization signature holds across the full dataset?

Can the authors explicitly state whether Pataskar et al.'s starvation-induced substitutions show the same stabilization signature in degradation data, or whether the mechanisms differ between starvation-induced and healthy-tissue substitutions?
For the U modification analysis, can the authors quantify the effect size of the modification–RAAS correlation and specify which U modifications (pseudouridine, dihydrouridine, other?) are involved?

weaknesses.text: **Causality from stability to abundance is not established.** The paper shows that high-RAAS substitutions have lower degradation rates (Fig. 3d, r < 10^−10), but this correlation does not prove that stability *causes* high abundance. The inverse relationship could equally reflect: (1) selection bias—only substitutions that happen to be stable enough to detect are observed, while destabilizing substitutions are degraded below detection limit; (2) reverse causality—high-abundance proteins may be more stable because they are more likely to fold correctly or be protected by binding partners; or (3) confounding—both stability and abundance may be driven by a third variable, such as codon optimality or mRNA structure, which affects both synthesis rate and degradation rate independently. The paper acknowledges detection bias (Discussion, 'lowly abundant substitutions are less likely to be identified') but does not address how this bias affects the causal interpretation of the stability–abundance relationship. To establish causality, the authors would need either: (a) a perturbation experiment (e.g., mutagenesis to destabilize a high-RAAS substitution and measure whether RAAS decreases), or (b) a more rigorous causal model that accounts for selection bias and competing mechanisms. As written, the claim that 'protein stability contributes to substitution abundance' (Abstract, Results heading) overstates what the correlation demonstrates.

**The mechanistic explanation for high RAAS relies on codon frequency and tRNA pairing, but alternative mechanisms are not adequately ruled out.** Figure 3a–b and Extended Data Fig. 4 show that RAAS correlates with codon-anticodon mismatches and codon frequency, consistent with a 'ribosomal misreading' model. However, the paper also identifies a strong association with RNA modifications (U modifications, p < 10^−10, Supplemental Fig. 8) and with sequence motifs (KRAQ, CC, MM, WW), yet does not test whether these motifs or modifications are sufficient to predict RAAS independently of codon frequency. If sequence context or RNA modifications are the primary drivers, then the codon-frequency effect may be spurious or secondary. The paper states (Discussion) that 'multiple mechanisms likely contribute,' but does not quantify their relative contributions or test whether they are independent. A multivariate model (e.g., logistic or linear regression) predicting RAAS from codon frequency, modification status, and motif presence would clarify which mechanisms dominate and whether codon frequency remains significant after controlling for modifications.

**The claim that 360 proteins have alternatively translated proteoforms as their most abundant form is not adequately supported by the evidence presented.** The paper identifies ~9,000 unique SAAP–BP pairs and reports that ~10% have RAAS > 1 (Fig. 2b), but the statement 'alternatively translated proteoforms are the most abundant protein products for 360 proteins' (Results, Quantification section) appears to conflate two different quantities: the number of unique substitution sites with RAAS > 1 and the number of proteins in which the substituted form is the dominant proteoform. If a protein has multiple substitution sites, only some of which have RAAS > 1, the protein-level abundance of the substituted form depends on which sites are included in the calculation. The paper computes 'protein RAAS' as the median RAAS across all SAAP in a protein (Methods, Protein set enrichment analysis), but does not clearly state how many proteins have median RAAS > 1, nor does it account for the possibility that different substitution sites in the same protein may be on different proteoforms (i.e., not all substitutions may occur on the same molecule). Figure 2h shows rank-sorted proteins with RAAS > 0.1, not RAAS > 1, and the text does not clearly distinguish between the two thresholds. Clarification of the protein-level calculation and a recount of proteins with median RAAS > 1 would resolve this.

The paper does not test whether the identified substitutions are functionally relevant or whether they alter protein activity; the claim that they 'diversify mammalian proteomes' is supported only by abundance and conservation, not by functional assays.

The ANOVA in Fig. 4f shows that substitution type explains the most variance in RAAS, but the model does not include codon frequency, RNA modifications, or sequence motifs as predictors, so it is unclear whether substitution type is a proxy for these mechanistic variables or an independent driver.

The prediction model (Fig. 5i) achieves a Pearson correlation of 0.44 between predicted and observed RAAS, which is modest; the paper does not discuss whether this is sufficient to claim that protein features 'successfully predict' RAAS or whether unmeasured variables dominate.

The conservation analysis (Fig. 5l–m) identifies only 55 identical SAAP sequences between human and mouse out of thousands, and the authors acknowledge this likely underestimates true conservation; however, the correlation of RAAS values for these 55 sites is presented as strong evidence of conservation, which may not generalize to the full set of substitutions.

The paper excludes SAAP from immunoglobulins and trypsin (Methods, Sequence confirmation) without quantifying how many sites were removed or justifying why these proteins are less likely to harbor genuine alternate translation events.

questions: In Fig. 3d, does the inverse correlation between RAAS and degradation rate hold within individual proteins, or only across the population of proteins? If the latter, could the correlation be driven by protein-level confounds (e.g., highly abundant proteins tend to be more stable and also more likely to have detectable substitutions)?
For the 360 proteins reported to have RAAS > 1, what is the median RAAS value and what fraction have median RAAS > 0.5 or > 0.1? How sensitive is this count to the choice of threshold?

Can the authors provide a multivariate regression model predicting RAAS from codon frequency, RNA modification status, and sequence motif presence, with standardized coefficients, to quantify the independent contribution of each mechanism?

What is the false-negative rate of the SAAP identification pipeline? The paper reports that ~40% of SAAP discovered by dependent peptide search were validated by standard database search, but does not estimate how many true SAAP were missed by the stringent filtering criteria.

weaknesses.text: The shared peptide test (Fig. 2d–e) does not definitively exclude the possibility that high-RAAS sites reflect a mixture of two proteoforms in which the substituted form is simply more abundant in a subset of cells or tissues, rather than the dominant form in most cells, and the histone ruler estimate (Fig. 2i) does not resolve whether high-RAAS proteoforms are the majority form in a single cell or a minority form present in many cells.

The absence of a variant in gnomAD does not prove a substitution is not genetic, only that it is rare or absent in the sequenced population, and the LSCC genome check covers only one cancer type and one patient cohort rather than a genome-wide check across all 1,000+ samples.

The manuscript does not report whether identified SAAP correspond to patient-matched genomic variants called from the same RNA-seq or WGS data, which would be a more direct test of genetic origin than gnomAD comparisons.

Codon frequency and tRNA pairing associations remain correlative; an alternative explanation is that sense codon recoding (via tRNA or mRNA modifications) preferentially occurs at rare codons, and the overlap between U modifications and substitution sites is modest (180 of 4,250 U in AAS codons) with unclear causal direction.

The manuscript would be stronger if it provided direct evidence that blocking or altering tRNA modifications reduces RAAS at specific sites, or that introducing modifications increases RAAS, rather than relying on correlative evidence.

The biological significance of most identified substitutions remains unclear—many have low RAAS and may be inconsequential, and the 360 proteins with RAAS > 1 represent a small fraction of the proteome with no estimate of what fraction of total protein mass or function is affected.

Functional claims are associative, not causal: enrichment of high-RAAS substitutions in signaling, proteolysis, and transcription (Fig. 5c) is suggestive but does not show that these substitutions alter function.

Tissue specificity is demonstrated but not mechanistically explained—the manuscript does not explain why some substitutions are tissue-specific (Extended Data Fig. 5h–i), whether due to differential tRNA expression, tissue-specific modifications, or cell-type-specific translation rates.

Cancer associations are weak: while some substitutions show higher RAAS in tumors (Fig. 5a–b), the overall signal is not strong (Extended Data Fig. 6a–b), and no causal link to tumorigenesis is demonstrated.

Cross-species conservation is limited in scope: only 55 of 1,102 mouse substitutions match human sequences exactly, and quantitative conservation analysis (e.g., homology-based matching) is not provided.

The KRAQ motif and other sequence patterns lack functional validation, and the authors note they 'cannot confidently rule out the possibility of multiple modifications' for these sites, which substantially weakens the claim.

Missing data bias is acknowledged but not fully addressed: low-RAAS substitutions on low-abundance proteins are less likely to be detected, potentially inflating median RAAS estimates for such proteins.

questions: Did you check whether any identified SAAP correspond to patient-matched genomic variants (SNVs/indels) called from the same RNA-seq data? If so, what fraction matched, and if not, why was this check not performed?

For the 360 proteins with RAAS > 1, what is the estimated fraction of total protein copies that are substituted versus canonical in a typical cell? The histone ruler estimate gives absolute copy numbers but not the ratio within each protein.

Can you provide quantitative evidence that sense codon recoding (via tRNA or mRNA modifications) contributes more to high-RAAS substitutions than codon misreading? The current evidence is correlative; a functional perturbation (e.g., blocking pseudouridylation) would be more convincing.

weaknesses.text: **Central claim—stability explains high RAAS—rests on correlative degradation data that cannot exclude confounding.** The authors show that substituted peptides with high RAAS have lower degradation rates than their base counterparts (Fig. 3d, r < 10^−10), and interpret this as evidence that substitutions stabilize proteins and thus accumulate. However, this correlation does not establish causation: a substitution could be abundant because it is synthesized at high rates (e.g., due to codon frequency or tRNA availability—mechanisms the authors themselves identify in Fig. 3a–b), and proteins synthesized at high rates may happen to be more stable due to selection against misfolding during rapid synthesis, or may occupy different cellular compartments or complexes that protect them. The authors state (Discussion) that 'protein stability variation is only one of the factors contributing to RAAS' and note 'the signal to noise in the degradation rates is smaller compared to the abundance measures,' but they do not test whether the observed degradation differences are a cause or a consequence of high RAAS. A direct perturbation (e.g., destabilizing the substituted form via mutation, or stabilizing the base form via synonymous codon optimization) would be needed to establish causation; the current data are consistent with it but do not prove it.

**Computational pipeline for identifying substitutions lacks sufficient procedural detail to reproduce the filtering and validation steps.** The dependent peptide search, validation search, and six filtering criteria (Methods, 'Candidate SAAP and PTM identification') are described in prose, but critical thresholds and decision logic are not fully specified: (1) the 'positional probability' threshold for assigning a mass shift to a single residue is not stated numerically; (2) the fragmentation-pattern comparison using Prosit (Supplemental Fig. 4) relies on cosine similarity, but the threshold for accepting a SAAP over an alternative hypothesis is not given; (3) the 6-frame translation filter (excluding sequences matching any genomic region) is described but the exact matching criteria (e.g., E-value, identity threshold) are not provided; (4) the 1% FDR 'computed only across SAAP' (Methods) is mentioned but the algorithm (target-decoy, permutation, or other) is not specified. Without these details, an independent group cannot reproduce the exact set of 8,801 substitution sites reported.

**Raw MS data availability is incomplete for reproducibility.** The manuscript states that CPTAC data were 'downloaded from NIH Proteomic Data Commons' and label-free data from 'dataset repository' (PXD010154, PXD030983), but does not confirm that all raw .raw files are publicly accessible at those repositories with no access restrictions. The Methods section does not state whether the authors have deposited their own processed data (e.g., MaxQuant evidence.txt, identified SAAP sequences with localization probabilities) in a public repository; Supplemental Data Tables are referenced but their availability is not explicitly confirmed. For the IP-MS validation (Supplemental Fig. 5), raw files are stated to be 'downloaded from the bioplex project' but no accession numbers are provided. Without confirmed public access to raw data and processed intermediate outputs (e.g., MaxQuant search results before filtering), independent verification of the filtering pipeline is not feasible.

**Custom Python scripts for mining DP search results and generating sample-specific databases are not deposited with version control or a DOI.** The Methods section references 'custom python scripts' and 'Galaxy-sourced python scripts' (e.g., gffcompare_to_bed.py, translate_bed.py, fasta_merge_files_and_filter_unique_sequences.py) but does not provide links to these scripts or confirm they are in the GitHub repository; the GitHub link (github.com/SlavovLab/decode) is mentioned but not verified to contain all scripts with clear version tags. The 'custom python scripts including functions adapted from ref. 13' for identifying AAS are particularly critical but are not separately documented. Without access to the exact code and version used, the filtering logic cannot be independently audited.

**Transcriptome assembly parameters and quality control thresholds are under-specified.** StringTie assembly is stated to use 'abundance at least 0.1% of the most abundant transcript at that locus' and 'at least 1 independent read,' but the impact of these thresholds on the final protein database is not quantified (e.g., how many transcripts were included/excluded, how does this affect the number of candidate SAAP?). The 'mean sequence coverage for all transcripts exceeds 98%' is reported, but per-sample coverage distributions and the number of transcripts with <98% coverage are not provided, making it unclear whether low-coverage regions could harbor undetected substitutions.

**Prosit intensity prediction and cosine similarity thresholds for fragmentation-pattern validation are not numerically specified.** Supplemental Fig. 4 shows examples of SAAP vs. alternative-hypothesis spectra compared by cosine similarity, but the threshold used to accept a SAAP (e.g., cosine > 0.7) is not stated in the Methods, and no sensitivity analysis (e.g., how many SAAP would be rejected if the threshold were raised) is provided.

**The 'histone ruler' copy-number estimation (Fig. 2i) assumes 30×10^6 histone copies per cell without justification or sensitivity analysis.** This estimate is critical for interpreting the biological significance of high-RAAS substitutions (hundreds to tens of thousands of copies per cell), but the source and variability of the 30×10^6 figure are not discussed, and no bounds on the estimate are provided.

**Statistical tests for RAAS comparisons across datasets and tissues use Welch's t-test on log-normal distributions without justification.** The Methods state that 'the global distribution of log10(RAAS) is approximately log-normal' and comparisons are made with 't-tests (Welch approximation),' but no normality test or justification for using t-tests on log-transformed data is provided; permutation tests or non-parametric alternatives might be more appropriate for skewed distributions.

**Load-bearing claim 1: High-RAAS substitutions reflect alternate translation, not alternative alleles or multiple modifications.** The authors exclude genetic variants by checking that LSCC patient genomes do not carry the relevant mutations (stated once, briefly). However, this is checked only for one cancer type, and the gnomAD analysis (Fig. 5j–k) shows that most alternate-translation codons have no observed variants—which is consistent with both the authors' claim and with the alternative that these sites are simply not polymorphic in the population, leaving the genetic origin hypothesis underdetermined. More critically, for ~half of all SAAP, the mass shift is not localized to a single position with high confidence (Methods: "for about half of all spectra matched to SAAP, the measured mass shift... cannot arise from multiple combinatorial modifications on different residues adding up to the mass shift; for the remaining SAAP, unknown combinatorial modifications cannot be rigorously disproved"). The authors argue that fragment ion intensities favor the proposed substitution over alternatives (Supplemental Fig. 4c–f), but this is a Bayesian argument: the predicted spectrum for Q→G is closer to observed than the predicted spectrum for cleavage, but both could be wrong, and the comparison does not rule out other modifications (e.g., simultaneous PTMs on different residues). The 2,000 high-confidence sites (positional probability >0.9) partially address this, but the main results (8,801 sites, 360 proteins with RAAS>1) include the lower-confidence set. The claim that these are "stable and abundant proteins" is thus supported for the high-confidence subset but overstated for the full dataset.

**Load-bearing claim 2: Protein stability is a major mechanism driving high RAAS.** The authors measure degradation rates in hepatocytes (Fig. 3c–f) and find that SAAP with high RAAS have lower degradation rates than their base peptides (inverse correlation, p<10^−10). However, this is correlational: slower degradation of a SAAP could reflect either (a) the substitution stabilizing the protein, or (b) the SAAP being a minor proteoform that is only detected when it is stable enough to accumulate—a selection bias. The authors acknowledge this indirectly ("sites on lowly abundant proteins with low RAAS are less likely to be detected") but do not fully disentangle it. The degradation analysis is also limited to hepatocytes and three other cell types; generalization to the full dataset (which includes cancer tissues) is not established. Moreover, the effect size is modest: the log-ratio of degradation rates for SAAP vs. BP is small (Fig. 3d), and the authors note "the signal to noise in the degradation rates is smaller compared to the abundance measures." This is consistent with stability contributing to RAAS, but it does not establish it as a primary driver for the high-RAAS proteins that motivate the paper.

**Load-bearing claim 3: These substitutions are conserved across species and functionally significant.** The authors identify 55 identical SAAP in human and mouse (Fig. 5l) and show their RAAS values correlate (p<10^−8). However, 55 shared sites out of 8,801 human sites is ~0.6% overlap, and the authors note this "likely underestimates the degree of conservation" due to sequence homology differences and technical factors. The correlation of RAAS for these 55 sites is real but does not establish that the broader set of human-specific substitutions are functional or conserved. The functional significance argument relies on GO enrichment (Fig. 5c) and association with cancer (Fig. 5a–b), but GO enrichment of high-RAAS proteins is not the same as showing those proteins have altered function due to the substitution—it shows they are in functional categories. The cancer-specific examples (lamin A, PP1-beta) are striking but anecdotal; no global test for cancer association is reported. The claim in the abstract that these results "demonstrate the contribution of alternate translation to diversifying mammalian proteomes" is supported for the identified substitutions but not for their functional impact.

The title claims substitutions result in "stable and abundant proteins," but abundance is measured as RAAS (ratio to canonical form), not absolute copy number; high RAAS does not necessarily mean high absolute abundance if the canonical form is also rare.

The abstract states "products of alternate translation are more abundant than their canonical counterparts for hundreds of proteins," but this is true only for ~360 proteins with RAAS>1 (Fig. 2h), and the confidence in this subset is lower for the broader dataset; the phrasing should specify the high-confidence subset or the RAAS threshold.

The claim that "substitution ratios are positively associated with intrinsically disordered regions" (abstract) is supported (Fig. 5h), but causality is not established—disorder may be a consequence of the substitution, not a predictor of where substitutions occur.

The paper does not report how many of the 8,801 sites would remain after applying the stringent filters used for the 2,000 high-confidence set; this would clarify how much of the main result depends on lower-confidence identifications.

The ANOVA analysis (Fig. 4f) shows substitution type explains more variance than tissue type, but the effect sizes are not reported, making it difficult to assess the biological importance of tissue-specific variation.

questions: For the ~4,000 SAAP with positional probability <0.9, what is the distribution of alternative hypotheses that could explain the observed mass shifts, and how often does the predicted spectrum for the proposed substitution rank first among all tested alternatives?

In the hepatocyte degradation data, what fraction of the inverse correlation between RAAS and degradation rate remains after controlling for protein abundance (which the authors note is correlated with both RAAS and detectability)?
How many of the 360 proteins with RAAS>1 in the full dataset would retain RAAS>1 if only high-confidence (positional probability >0.9) SAAP were included?
For the 55 conserved SAAP between human and mouse, what is the range of RAAS values, and do they cluster in the high-RAAS or low-RAAS tail of the distribution?
